# Cloe — Claude Call: 3-day prototype plan and spec

Oct 24, 2026 · @palak

## Overview

## Overview

Cloe is a local app that lets you talk to Claude Code and hear it talk back. You hold a key, say what you want, and Cloe forwards it to a Claude Code session running on your subscription. Replies come back as speech, with an on-screen text panel in visual mode and no panel in audio-only mode. A `claude-call` skill reshapes each reply into something that works for the ear instead of the eye.

The prototype has three days to prove the loop end to end: push to talk, Claude Code answers, Cloe speaks a short sensible reply, the user can interrupt, and the whole thing runs on the existing Claude subscription with no extra API keys. It is scoped to discussion and planning, not file edits, so it needs no approval UI in v0. Success is a two-minute live demo where a non-technical observer can follow the conversation.

## Scope

## Scope

In scope for v0:

- Push-to-talk voice input from a local web page, running in Chrome or Edge
- A single conversation per session, resumed across turns through `claude -p --resume`
- Spoken replies through the browser's own speech synthesis, started sentence by sentence as Claude writes
- Visual+Audio mode (text panel visible) and Audio-only mode (panel hidden), toggled from the page
- A `claude-call` skill that controls the spoken style and the output tag format
- A deterministic cleanup pass that catches markdown, code, paths, URLs and symbols that slip past the skill
- Local control vocabulary: "Cloe stop", "Cloe repeat", "Cloe shorter", "switch to audio mode"
- Barge-in: speaking over Cloe stops the current audio and the running turn
- Spoken tool-event narration ("reading auth dot ts") while Claude works
- Read-only Claude Code session (`--permission-mode plan`), so there are no destructive actions to approve

Out of scope for v0:

- VS Code extension (web page is simpler and avoids extension-host mic issues)
- Real streaming STT or TTS vendors (browser APIs are good enough for the demo)
- An always-on wake word (push-to-talk is enough; a soft wake word is a Day 3 stretch)
- Voice-driven approvals for file edits or shell commands
- Memory across sessions beyond `--resume` within one run
- Packaging, installer, auth, multi-user
- A second rewriter model; the skill plus the cleaner do the language work on the single Claude call

## Architecture

## Architecture

&#91;embedded content: Cloe pipeline · 9 components, one Claude Code session\]

The top row carries your voice to Claude; the middle row carries Claude's reply back out as speech. The server is a thin Node process that owns the WebSocket to the page and spawns one `claude -p` child per conversation, resuming it with `--resume` between turns. Everything in the top and middle rows is yours; `claude -p` is unchanged, with the `claude-call` skill picked up from the server's working directory. The screen panel is only shown in Visual+Audio mode and reads the `<screen>` block from each reply.

## Interaction model

## Interaction model

One person, one microphone, one conversation at a time. The page has three states: listening, thinking, speaking. The current state is always visible as a label beside the mic indicator, so the user never wonders if Cloe heard them.

Turn-taking rules:

- **Hold space to talk.** Release to send. A 200 ms lead-in avoids the first-word drop that Chromium speech recognition sometimes shows.
- **Barge-in cuts Cloe off.** Starting to talk while Cloe is speaking stops the audio immediately, kills the running `claude -p` child, and starts a new turn. There is no setting for this; it is always on.
- **One question at a time.** Cloe ends each reply with a clear hand-back ("want me to go deeper?") or

import type { Mode } from "./types.ts";

const CONTRACTIONS: [RegExp, string][] = [
  [/\bcan't\b/gi, "cannot"],
  [/\bwon't\b/gi, "will not"],
  [/\bdon't\b/gi, "do not"],
  [/\bdoesn't\b/gi, "does not"],
  [/\bisn't\b/gi, "is not"],
  [/\baren't\b/gi, "are not"],
  [/\bwasn't\b/gi, "was not"],
  [/\bdidn't\b/gi, "did not"],
  [/\bshouldn't\b/gi, "should not"],
];

function splitWords(s: string): string {
  return s
    .replace(/([a-z0-9])([A-Z])/g, "$1 $2")
    .replace(/([A-Z]+)([A-Z][a-z])/g, "$1 $2")
    .replace(/_/g, " ");
}

function fileName(path: string): string {
  const base = path.split("/").filter(Boolean).pop() ?? path;
  return base.replace(/\./g, " dot ");
}

/** Deterministic cleanup for anything headed to the TTS queue. */
export function clean(text: string, mode: Mode = "visual"): string {
  let t = text;
  t = t.replace(/```[\s\S]*?```/g, () =>
    mode === "visual" ? " I have left a code snippet on screen. " : " the code is in a file I can save. ",
  );
  t = t.replace(/`([^`]+)`/g, "$1");
  t = t.replace(/https?:\/\/\S+/g, "a link");
  t = t.replace(/(?:\.{0,2}\/)?(?:[\w@.-]+\/)+[\w@.-]+/g, (m) => fileName(m));
  t = t.replace(/^\s{0,3}#{1,6}\s+/gm, "");
  t = t.replace(/^\s*[-*+]\s+/gm, "");
  t = t.replace(/^\s*\d+[.)]\s+/gm, "");
  t = t.replace(/^\s*\|?[\s:|-]{3,}\|?\s*$/gm, "");
  t = t.replace(/\|/g, ", ");
  t = t.replace(/(\*\*|__|\*|_(?=\S))/g, "");
  t = t.replace(/\be\.g\./gi, "for example").replace(/\bi\.e\./gi, "that is");
  t = t.replace(/->|=>/g, " to ").replace(/&/g, " and ");
  t = t.replace(/\b[a-z]+(?:[A-Z][a-z0-9]*)+\b|\b\w+_\w+\b/g, splitWords);
  t = t.replace(/\b(\w+) dot (ts|js|py|md|json)\b/g, "$1 dot $2");
  for (const [re, rep] of CONTRACTIONS) t = t.replace(re, rep);
  t = t.replace(/[#*~^<>{}[\]\\]/g, " ");
  return t.replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim();
}

/** Split text into sentences; the trailing fragment is returned as rest. */
export function splitSentences(text: string): { sentences: string[]; rest: string } {
  const sentences: string[] = [];
  const re = /[^.!?\n]+(?:[.!?]+|\n)(?=\s|$)/g;
  let last = 0;
  let m: RegExpExecArray | null;
  while ((m = re.exec(text))) {
    const s = m[0].trim();
    if (s) sentences.push(s);
    last = re.lastIndex;
  }
  return { sentences, rest: text.slice(last) };
}

import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { cp, mkdir, readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { extname, join, normalize } from "node:path";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";
import { WebSocketServer, type WebSocket } from "ws";
import { ClaudeAgent } from "./agent.ts";
import { clean } from "./cleaner.ts";
import { narrate } from "./narration.ts";
import { ReplyParser } from "./parser.ts";
import type { Agent, Mode, Rewriter } from "./types.ts";

const root = fileURLToPath(new URL("..", import.meta.url));
const webDir = join(root, "web");
const sessionDir = join(root, "session");
const PORT = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const TYPES: Record<string, string> = { ".html": "text/html", ".js": "text/javascript", ".css": "text/css" };

const rewriter: Rewriter = { toSpeech: async (x) => x };

async function plantSkill() {
  const dest = join(sessionDir, ".claude", "skills", "claude-call");
  await mkdir(dest, { recursive: true });
  await cp(join(root, "skill", "claude-call"), dest, { recursive: true });
}

const http = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const path = normalize(req.url === "/" || !req.url ? "/index.html" : req.url.split("?")[0]).replace(/^(\.\.[/\\])+/, "");
  try {
    const body = await readFile(join(webDir, path));
    res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": TYPES[extname(path)] ?? "application/octet-stream" }).end(body);
  } catch {
    res.writeHead(404).end("not found");
  }
});

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server: http });

wss.on("connection", (ws: WebSocket) => {
  const agent: Agent = new ClaudeAgent(sessionDir);
  let sessionId: string | undefined;
  let turn = 0;
  const send = (m: object) => ws.readyState === ws.OPEN && ws.send(JSON.stringify(m));

  async function runTurn(text: string, mode: Mode) {
    agent.interrupt();
    const me = ++turn;
    const alive = () => me === turn;
    const parser = new ReplyParser();
    const prefix = mode === "audio" ? "[mode: audio-only]" : "[mode: visual+audio]";
    send({ type: "state", state: "thinking" });
    const emit = async (events: ReturnType<ReplyParser["feed"]>) => {
      for (const e of events) {
        if (!alive()) return;
        if (e.kind === "screen") send({ type: "screen", text: e.text });
        else if (e.kind === "sentence") {
          const s = clean(await rewriter.toSpeech(e.text), mode);
          if (s) send({ type: "speak", text: s });
        } else {
          const cleaned = clean(await rewriter.toSpeech(e.text), mode);
          const parts = cleaned.match(/[^.!?]+[.!?]*/g) ?? [];
          for (const s of parts.slice(0, 3)) send({ type: "speak", text: s.trim() });
          if (parts.length > 3) send({ type: "screen", text: e.text });
        }
      }
    };
    try {
      for await (const ev of agent.send(`${prefix} ${text}`, sessionId)) {
        if (!alive()) return;
        if (ev.kind === "text") await emit(parser.feed(ev.text));
        else if (ev.kind === "tool") {
          const n = narrate(ev.name, ev.input);
          if (n) send({ type: "narrate", text: n });
        } else if (ev.kind === "done") sessionId = ev.sessionId || sessionId;
      }
      await emit(parser.end());
      if (alive()) send({ type: "done" });
    } catch (err) {
      if (alive()) send({ type: "error", text: `Cloe hit a problem: ${(err as Error).message}` });
    }
  }

  ws.on("message", (raw) => {
    let m: any;
    try { m = JSON.parse(String(raw)); } catch { return; }
    if (m.type === "prompt" && typeof m.text === "string") {
      send({ type: "screen-reset" });
      void runTurn(m.text, m.mode === "audio" ? "audio" : "visual");
    } else if (m.type === "interrupt") {
      turn++;
      agent.interrupt();
      send({ type: "state", state: "idle" });
    }
  });
  ws.on("close", () => { turn++; agent.interrupt(); });
});

await plantSkill();

I've built the first version of Cloe. I tested the server against the real claude CLI. I haven't tried the browser page: it needs a mic and Chrome or Edge, so it's untested.

What I ran - A scripted client sent one prompt over the WebSocket. The server returned the thinking state, then five spoken sentences, a streamed screen block and done. - The three unit tests pass. They cover the reply parser (including tags split mid-chunk, and the missing-tag fallback) and the cleaner.

What's in it - Server (server/): - index.ts serves the page and runs the WebSocket. It copies the skill into session/.claude/skills/ on start. - agent.ts runs one claude -p child per turn in plan mode, resuming with --resume. - parser.ts and cleaner.ts split replies into spoken sentences and a screen block, and clean up markdown, code, paths and URLs. - narration.ts speaks short phrases while Claude uses tools. - types.ts holds the Agent, STT, TTS and Rewriter interfaces from the spec. - Skill (skill/claude-call/): SKILL.md, examples.md (8 pairs) and condensation.md. The spec asks for 10 to 15 example pairs, so that file needs more. - Page (web/): hold space to talk, with a lead-in and tail around the hold. Speech recognition and speech synthesis both run in the browser. It shows the state label, a visual/audio toggle and the screen panel. The voice commands (stop, repeat, shorter, switch mode) are handled in the page. Speaking over Cloe cuts it off and kills the running turn.

To run it: npm start, then open http://localhost:3000 in Chrome or Edge.

Things to know - The code is TypeScript that Node 24 runs directly, so there's no build step. - Cloe only handles "switch to visual mode" when it hears the word "visual", so it may mishear the command. - The spec's last four sections (Three-day plan, Risks, Demo script, Roadmap) are empty headings, so I had nothing to build from for those.

add this in a summarized wqy in the appropriate section in the SPEC"can we do the following, jave the always on wake word active only when the session has been manually started. so if a person starts the session the transcriber will run, it runs for 15 mins , and after any break of more than 15 mins of the last spoken command to claude(changeable amount of sleep time) it stops running the transcriber this will be less heavier on the battery. also can we choose a better word instead of CLOE - a word well designed so that it is less likely to be misheard. - response - Yes, both work well, and together they neatly solve the usual "always-on is too heavy, push-to-talk is too clunky" trade-off. ## The session model you're describing Call it a **listening window**. The user explicitly starts it (button or key); the recognizer runs; every detected utterance containing the wake word resets a 15-minute inactivity timer. When the timer expires with no new wake-word hit, the recognizer stops and Cloe goes to sleep. The user starts another window to resume. This is better than true always-on in three ways. The user has intent — they chose to start a session, so false triggers in the background are rare because they're at the keyboard. Battery stays bounded; a session with a quiet 15 minutes dies on its own. And there's no "did I leave the mic on?" worry, because the state is explicit and visible. A few details worth settling now so Day 2 doesn't drift: - **The timer resets on wake-word hits, not on all speech.** Otherwise a nearby conversation keeps Cloe alive forever. The whole point of the wake word is that it's the one signal the user is actually talking *to* Cloe. - **Sleep is loud, not silent.** When the timer fires, Cloe says one short line ("going to sleep, say the word to wake me") and the mic indicator turns off. Silent sleep is a confusing bug. - **Reset also happens on a reply.** If Cloe is still speaking when the timer would fire, hold the timer until she's done plus a short grace (say 30 seconds), so a long answer doesn't trap the user in a dead session. - **Inactivity is configurable.** `sleepMinutes: 15` in the config, surfaced as a slider on the page later. Values from 2 to 60 are reasonable; under 2 is annoying, over 60 defeats the purpose. - **An explicit stop command.** "Go to sleep" ends the window immediately without waiting for the timer. Pairs with the start button. - **State is visible.** Three states on the page: `asleep` (gray dot), `listening for wake word` (soft blue dot), `active` (solid blue dot, during and just after a wake-word utterance). Users should never have to guess which one they're in. I'd put the always-on recognizer behind a `WakeListener` interface alongside the four already in the spec, so you can swap the browser recognizer for Porcupine later without touching the state machine. ## The name Cloe has a real problem: "C" and "K" sounds are among the hardest for speech recognizers, and short two-syllable names collide with common words (clone, close, slow, below). "Cloe" also lands near "close", which is a disaster for a voice assistant where "close that" is a plausible command. What makes a good wake word, so the picks aren't arbitrary: - **Three syllables or more.** Two-syllable words trigger too often; one-syllable words miss too often. "Alexa" is four syllables. "OK Google" is three. "Hey Siri" is three. - **Unusual phoneme sequence.** The word shouldn't sound like any common English word, especially not any likely command. - **Open vowels early.** Vowels like /a/, /o/, /e/ are easier to pick out of background noise than closed /i/ or /u/. - **Hard consonant start.** A plosive (p, t, k) or affricate (ch, j) at the start gives the detector a clear onset. "Alexa" opens with a vowel and that's one reason it has the highest false-trigger rate of the major wake words. - **No common homophones.** No "Siri / Sear / Seer / Syria" problem. - **Not already a wake word.** You don't want users triggering their phone while talking to Cloe. Candidates that fit, picked for the voice-coding context: - **Codex** — three syllables, hard /k/ opener, /d/ and /ks/ in the middle, no common homophone, obviously tech-coded. One concern: OpenAI uses "Codex" as a product name, which may be confusing in a coding tool. - **Juno** — two syllables but very distinct: /dʒ/ onset, open /u/ and /o/, no common commands collide. Pleasant to say. Risk: a bit short. - **Pilot** — three syllables if you say it slowly, open vowels, hard /p/ start, meaningful ("co-pilot" for coding). Risk: collides with Microsoft Copilot. - **Ada** — three syllables, open vowels throughout, /d/ in the middle for a clean break, nice nod to Ada Lovelace. Risk: short, and "a-duh" could blur into natural speech. - **Echo** — one problem: it's Amazon's device name, so Alexa triggers. - **Oracle** — three syllables, strong /k/ and /l/ in the middle, open vowels, no command collision. Risk: Oracle the company. - **Atlas** — two syllables but phonetically distinct: open /a/, hard /tl/ cluster, hard /s/ ending. Common word but rarely a command. My pick would be **Codex** if the OpenAI overlap doesn't bother you, otherwise **Juno**. Both score well on all the technical criteria and are the kind of name you can comfortably say out loud in a demo without feeling silly. If you want to go a different direction entirely, two more worth considering: **Cursor** (collides with the IDE), **Mentor** (slightly bland), or an invented word like **Noma** or **Veya** (zero collision risk but no meaning hook). Want me to update the spec with the listening-window model and a chosen name? ## Interaction model

One person, one microphone, one conversation at a time. The page has three states: listening, thinking, speaking. The current state is always visible as a label beside the mic indicator, so the user never wonders if Oluna heard them.

Turn-taking rules:

- **Hold space to talk.** Release to send. A 200 ms lead-in avoids the first-word drop that Chromium speech recognition sometimes shows.
- **Barge-in cuts Oluna off.** Starting to talk while Oluna is speaking stops the audio immediately, kills the running `claude -p` child, and starts a new turn. There is no setting for this; it is always on.
- **One question at a time.** Oluna ends each reply with a clear hand-back ("want me to go deeper?") or a short status ("done, over to you"), so the user knows the turn is theirs.

Listening window (Day 3 stretch, replaces always-on):

The wake word is active only after the user manually starts a session (button or key). The recognizer runs for that window and stops on its own, which keeps battery use bounded and avoids "did I leave the mic on?" worry.

- **Inactivity timer.** The window ends after `sleepMinutes` (default 15, configurable, sensible range 2 to 60) with no wake-word utterance. Only wake-word hits reset the timer, not all speech, so a nearby conversation cannot keep Oluna alive.
- **Hold while speaking.** If Oluna is still speaking when the timer would fire, it waits until she finishes plus a 30 second grace.
- **Loud sleep.** On expiry Oluna says one short line ("going to sleep, say the word to wake me") and the mic indicator turns off. "Go to sleep" ends the window immediately.
- **Visible state.** `asleep` (gray dot), `listening for wake word` (soft blue), `active` (solid blue, during and just after a wake-word utterance). This sits beside the listening, thinking, speaking labels.

Modes:

- **Visual+Audio** shows the text panel on the right and the speech plays on the left. The `<screen>` block is rendered as markdown; the `<spoken>` block is read aloud. Oluna can refer to the screen ("the diff is on the right").
- **Audio-only** hides the panel entirely. The skill switches to a variant that never points at the screen and offers to save detail to a file instead. The toggle is a single button and a voice command.

Wake word:

The name is **Oluna**. It has three syllables, open vowels, a distinctive phoneme sequence, and no common homophone or command collision, which suits a wake word. It replaces the earlier working name, which sounded too much like "close".

The name Oluna:

- Oluna is the voice of Claude Call. It is the name on the page title, the listening indicator, and the error messages ("Oluna couldn't hear that").
- Oluna refers to herself sparingly in replies; the skill tells Claude to use the first person and only self-name when it reads naturally.
- The TTS voice is fixed per OS: Samantha on macOS, Google UK English Female on Chrome Windows. Voice consistency does more for the "feels like Oluna" effect than the name itself.

## Interaction model

## Interaction model

One person, one microphone, one conversation at a time. The page shows the current state beside the mic indicator, so the user never wonders if Oluna heard them: `asleep` (gray), `listening` (blue, waiting for the wake word), `thinking`, `speaking`.

Listening window:

- **Manual start.** The user starts a window with a button or key. Outside a window the recognizer is off, so there is no background battery drain.
- **Wake word.** Within a window, speech that begins with "Oluna" is sent on; everything else is ignored.
- **Sleep timer.** The window ends after `sleepMinutes` (default 15, user-adjustable, 2 to 60) with no "Oluna" utterance. Only wake-word hits reset the timer. If Oluna is mid-reply, the timer waits until the reply ends plus 30 seconds.
- **Loud sleep.** On expiry Oluna says "going to sleep, say start to wake me" and the indicator goes gray. "Oluna, go to sleep" ends the window immediately.

Turn-taking rules:

- **Barge-in cuts Oluna off.** Saying "Oluna" while Oluna is speaking stops the audio, kills the running `claude -p` child, and starts a new turn. It is always on.
- **One question at a time.** Oluna ends each reply with a clear hand-back ("want me to go deeper?") or a short status ("done, over to you").

Modes:

- **Visual+Audio** shows the text panel on the right and the speech plays on the left. The `<screen>` block is rendered as markdown; the `<spoken>` block is read aloud. Oluna can refer to the screen ("the diff is on the right").
- **Audio-only** hides the panel entirely. The skill switches to a variant that never points at the screen and offers to save detail to a file instead. The toggle is a single button and a voice command.

The name Oluna:

- Oluna is chosen as the wake word: three syllables, open vowels, no common homophone, and unlike the earlier working name it does not sound like "close".
- Oluna is the voice of Claude Call. It is the name on the page title, the listening indicator, and the error messages ("Oluna couldn't hear that").
- Oluna refers to herself sparingly in replies; the skill tells Claude to use the first person and only self-name when it reads naturally.
- The TTS voice is fixed per OS: Samantha on macOS, Google UK English Female on Chrome Windows. Voice consistency does more for the "feels like Oluna" effect than the name itself.

Local control vocabulary (handled by the harness without a round trip):

- `stop` / `Oluna stop` — stop speaking and the running turn
- `repeat` / `Oluna repeat that` — replay the last spoken block
- `shorter` / `Oluna shorter` — ask Claude for the shorter version of the last answer
- `switch to audio mode` / `switch to visual mode` — flip the panel

Everything else is forwarded as a prompt.
138:- The spoken block is split on sentence boundaries and pushed to the TTS queue as each sentence closes, so playback starts before Claude finishes writing.
139:- The screen block is pushed to the page as a stream and rendered as markdown.

Probably not reliably. I haven't tested it in Safari, so this is from what I know of its speech support.

  • Speech output: speechSynthesis works in Safari, so Oluna could talk back. The spec's preferred macOS voice, Samantha, is available there.
  • Speech input: this is the problem.
  • Safari has webkitSpeechRecognition, so the page's check for it would pass. Its continuous mode is unreliable, though.
  • It tends to stop on its own, and each restart can bring up a mic permission prompt.
  • It also relies on Siri and dictation being enabled in macOS.
  • The listening window depends on long-running continuous recognition, so it would likely break.
  • Chrome-only features: interim results, which Oluna uses for fast barge-in, are patchy in Safari. The spec also names the "Google UK English Female" voice for Windows Chrome.

For the demo, use Chrome or Edge, as the spec says. To support Safari properly we'd swap the STT interface for a server-side one, such as the Gemini transcription the spec lists as a swap-in. That would also work in any browser, but it needs an API key.

Turn 15

what speech to text model will we use ?
Claude's response

No separate model of our own. The current speech-to-text is the browser's built-in Web Speech API (SpeechRecognition) in Chrome or Edge. It runs behind the scenes on the browser vendor's service. In Chrome that service is Google's cloud, which is why a network error can appear.

Why it's the default - No API keys or cost: the spec asks for the prototype to run on the existing Claude subscription with nothing extra. - Streaming: it gives live partial results, which we use for the fast "Oluna" barge-in. - Small code: it's about 30 lines in web/app.js.

Downsides - Accuracy on "Oluna": it's a made-up word, so the recognizer may mishear it. That is why the code accepts a few variants. - Audio goes to the browser vendor: don't use it for sensitive speech. - Keeps working only while Chrome allows it: it is a continuous session that Chrome sometimes ends, so the code restarts it.

Swap-ins (the spec keeps STT and WakeListener as interfaces for this reason) - Gemini transcribe: gemini-3.5-transcribe or the live version, which is more accurate but needs a Gemini API key. The spec notes its free tier uses your audio to improve Google products. - Local models: Whisper through a local server needs no cloud. For the wake word alone, Porcupine can detect "Oluna" on-device, and a custom word is easy to train there.

If the browser recognizer keeps missing "Oluna", the best fix is probably an on-device wake word, with the browser STT only used after the wake word. Want me to wait for your test results first?

How it works now - Sending: click Start session and just talk. Short pauses are merged into one turn, and about 1.2 seconds of silence sends it to Claude. - Interrupting: talking over Buddy cuts its audio and the running reply at once. - Commands: "stop", "repeat", "shorter", "switch to audio mode" and "go to sleep" work as plain phrases, with no "Buddy" in front. "Stop" and "go to sleep" are sent immediately. - Sleep timer: it now resets on any speech from you and ends after the sleep time with none. It still waits for a reply in progress plus 30 seconds, and the 2 to 60 minute setting is unchanged. - Echo guard: the mic also hears your speakers, so Buddy could answer itself. The page ignores any transcript that mostly repeats words from its current reply, and the "heard:" line marks it "ignored: my own voice". Headphones are still the reliable fix.

Spec: I rewrote the listening window section and removed the wake word from the scope, the state labels and the commands. I also dropped the WakeListener interface, because STT now covers it. "Buddy" is only the agent's name.

Caveats - Background noise or someone else talking will now get sent as prompts, because nothing filters for you. - The echo guard is word-matching, so a short reply could slip through on speakers.

Reload with Ctrl+Shift+R, click Start session, and try a conversation. If it triggers on its own voice or noise, tell me what the "heard:" line shows and I'll tune the filter.

# Buddy v2: make it feel like a phone call

## Context

The current page is still turn-based. Chrome's `SpeechRecognition` cuts off half of what the user says: it finalizes early, and its restarts drop audio. Buddy only speaks once a reply arrives, and every turn cold-starts a new `claude -p`, so the waits are long. The user wants a **call**:
- just talk; when you stop, it goes to Claude
- Buddy talks *while* Claude works
- the screen shows thinking and tool activity live
- "pause" stops Buddy instantly, and Claude is told where you paused and what you missed
- Claude works as a normal agent (auto permission mode) but speaks short, crisp, conversational lines

User decisions: no API keys and no separate model server if at all avoidable. Keep the browser voice for TTS. Permission mode is `auto`. Pause means **hold**: Claude keeps working and "go on" resumes.

## Approach

### 1. Listening: VAD endpointing + in-browser transcription (no key, no server)
Every good speech-to-text engine is a model or a cloud service. The no-key, no-server option is **npm packages that run small models inside the browser**, downloaded once and cached. They run on the user's laptop, not this server.
- **`@ricky0123/vad-web` (Silero VAD, ~2 MB)** decides when the user starts and stops talking. This fixes the cut-offs. The turn ends after ~700 ms of real silence (tunable), not when Chrome guesses. It captures the *whole* utterance audio with no restart gaps. The mic uses `getUserMedia({echoCancellation:true})`.
- **`@huggingface/transformers` + Moonshine base (ONNX, ~60 MB, WebGPU/WASM)** transcribes each finished segment in ~200–500 ms. Both load from jsDelivr with pinned versions, so the server needs no build step.
- **Fallback:** if the model fails to load, use the current Chrome recognizer behind the same `STT` interface (`server/types.ts`), and say so on screen.
- Live captions show "listening…" with a VAD level meter while the user speaks, then the transcript when the segment closes.

### 2. Barge-in and pause: duck first, decide after
- **VAD speech-start while Buddy speaks:** pause TTS immediately (`speechSynthesis.pause()`, with cancel-and-requeue as a fallback). Record the exact position: sentence index plus the word char index from `onboundary`, or sentence-level when the voice gives no boundaries.
- **When the segment is transcribed:**
  - `pause` / `hold on` / `wait` → stay paused. Show "Paused at '…'". Claude keeps streaming into a buffer.
  - `go on` / `continue` / `resume` → resume from the paused word, then keep playing the buffer live.
  - noise or empty → auto-resume after ~300 ms.
  - anything else → **interrupt** with context (§4).
- `stop`, `repeat`, `shorter`, the mode switches and `go to sleep` stay local commands (from `handle()` in `web/app.js`).

### 3. Agent: one warm Claude process per call
Rewrite `server/agent.ts` → `ClaudeSession`:
- **Spawn once per call:** `claude -p --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages --permission-mode auto --append-system-prompt-file skill/claude-call/VOICE.md`. Each user message is a JSON line on stdin, so there is no cold start per turn.
- **Events:** `say-text` deltas, `thinking` deltas, `tool` (name and input), `tool_result` (short summary), `done`. Keep the `AgentEvent` union in `server/types.ts` and extend it.
- **Interrupt:** send the stream-json `control_request` `{subtype:"interrupt"}`. If that turns out unsupported, fall back to kill and respawn with `--resume <sessionId>` (the session id is already tracked). Verify this first.
- **Cwd:** the user's chosen project dir via `BUDDY_CWD`, defaulting to `session/`, so `auto` mode edits a project and not the app itself.

### 4. Conversational output contract (replaces `<spoken>`)
New `skill/claude-call/VOICE.md`, appended as a system prompt. The marker trick is dropped. It is built from the existing `SKILL.md`, `examples.md` and `condensation.md`.
- Work like a normal agent. Speak only insi

import { createInterface } from "node:readline";
const c = spawn("claude", ["-p","--input-format","stream-json","--output-format","stream-json","--verbose","--include-partial-messages","--permission-mode","auto"], { stdio: ["pipe","pipe","pipe"] });
c.stderr.on("data", d => process.stdout.write("ERR " + d));
const t0 = Date.now(); let n = 0;
const send = (text) => c.stdin.write(JSON.stringify({ type: "user", message: { role: "user", content: text } }) + "\n");
createInterface({ input: c.stdout }).on("line", (l) => {
  const e = JSON.parse(l); const ms = Date.now() - t0;
  if (e.type === "stream_event") { const d = e.event?.delta; if (d?.type === "thinking_delta") process.stdout.write(""); if (e.event.type==="content_block_start") console.log(ms, "block_start", e.event.content_block.type); return; }

  if (e.type === "result") { n++; if (n === 1) { send("Count slowly from 1 to 200, one number per line."); setTimeout(() => { console.log("-- interrupt"); c.stdin.write(JSON.stringify({ type: "control_request", request_id: "r1", request: { subtype: "interrupt" } }) + "\n"); }, 4000); } else if (n === 2) { send("Say just: ok"); } else { c.stdin.end(); } }
});
send("Say just: hi");

setTimeout(() => { console.log("timeout"); c.kill(); }, 110000);

export type AgentEvent =
  | { kind: "text"; text: string }
  | { kind: "thinking"; text: string }
  | { kind: "tool"; id: string; name: string; input: unknown }
  | { kind: "tool_result"; id: string; ok: boolean; summary: string }
  | { kind: "permission"; name: string; input: unknown }
  | { kind: "done"; sessionId: string; interrupted: boolean }
  | { kind: "error"; message: string };

/** A long-lived agent conversation: one warm process per call, one message per turn. */
export interface Agent {
  start(): void;
  /** Queue a user message; returns its turn number. Interrupts the running turn first. */
  send(text: string): number;
  interrupt(): void;
  close(): void;
  on(listener: (turn: number, event: AgentEvent) => void): void;
}

/** Speech to text for one finished utterance (16 kHz mono samples in -1..1). */
export interface STT {
  ready(): Promise<void>;
  transcribe(audio: Float32Array): Promise<string>;
}

export interface TTS {
  speak(sentence: string): Promise<void>;
  stop(): void;
}

export interface Rewriter {
  toSpeech(text: string): Promise<string>;
}

export type Mode = "visual" | "audio";

cat > server/agent.ts <<'EOF'
import { spawn, type ChildProcess } from "node:child_process";
import { createInterface } from "node:readline";
import type { Agent, AgentEvent } from "./types.ts";

type Listener = (turn: number, event: AgentEvent) => void;

/**
 * One warm `claude -p` process per call, fed user messages as stream-json on stdin.
 * Turns run one at a time; sending while busy interrupts the running turn first.
 */
export class ClaudeSession implements Agent {
  private child: ChildProcess | null = null;
  private listeners: Listener[] = [];
  private queue: { turn: number; text: string }[] = [];
  private active = 0; // turn currently running in Claude, 0 when idle
  private interrupted = new Set<number>();
  private turns = 0;
  private sessionId = "";
  private streamed = false;
  private cwd: string;
  private systemPrompt: string;
  private permissionMode: string;

  constructor(opts: { cwd: string; systemPrompt: string; permissionMode?: string }) {
    this.cwd = opts.cwd;
    this.systemPrompt = opts.systemPrompt;
    this.permissionMode = opts.permissionMode ?? "auto";
  }

  on(listener: Listener): void {
    this.listeners.push(listener);
  }

  start(): void {
    if (this.child) return;
    const args = [
      "-p", "--input-format", "stream-json", "--output-format", "stream-json",
      "--verbose", "--include-partial-messages",
      "--permission-mode", this.permissionMode,
      "--append-system-prompt", this.systemPrompt,
      ...(this.sessionId ? ["--resume", this.sessionId] : []),
    ];
    const child = spawn("claude", args, { cwd: this.cwd, stdio: ["pipe", "pipe", "pipe"] });
    this.child = child;
    let stderr = "";
    child.stderr!.on("data", (d) => (stderr = (stderr + d).slice(-2000)));
    child.stdin!.on("error", () => {});
    createInterface({ input: child.stdout! }).on("line", (line) => this.onLine(line));
    child.on("close", (code) => {
      if (this.child !== child) return;
      this.child = null;
      const turn = this.active;
      this.active = 0;
      if (turn) this.emit(turn, { kind: "error", message: stderr.trim().split("\n").pop() || `Claude exited (${code})` });
      if (turn) this.emit(turn, { kind: "done", sessionId: this.sessionId, interrupted: true });
      this.pump();
    });
  }

  send(text: string): number {
    const turn = ++this.turns;
    // newest message wins: drop anything still waiting and cut the running turn
    for (const q of this.queue) this.interrupted.add(q.turn);
    this.queue = [{ turn, text }];
    if (this.active) this.interrupt();
    this.pump();
    return turn;
  }

  interrupt(): void {
    if (!this.active || !this.child) return;
    this.interrupted.add(this.active);
    this.write({ type: "control_request", request_id: `int-${this.active}`, request: { subtype: "interrupt" } });
  }

cat >> server/narration.ts <<'EOF'

const short = (s: unknown, n = 48) => {
  const t = typeof s === "string" ? s.replace(/\s+/g, " ").trim() : "";
  return t.length > n ? t.slice(0, n - 1) + "…" : t;
};
const file = (p: unknown) => (typeof p === "string" ? p.split("/").pop() ?? p : "");

/** Compact on-screen label for a tool card, e.g. "Read · auth.ts". */
export function toolLabel(name: string, input: unknown): string {
  const i = (input ?? {}) as Record<string, unknown>;
  const detail =
    i.file_path ? file(i.file_path) :
    i.notebook_path ? file(i.notebook_path) :
    name === "Bash" ? short(i.description || i.command) :
    i.pattern ? `“${short(i.pattern, 32)}”` :
    i.query ? `“${short(i.query, 32)}”` :
    i.url ? short(i.url) :
    i.description ? short(i.description) : "";
  return detail ? `${name} · ${detail}` : name;
}
EOF

cat > skill/claude-call/VOICE.md <<'EOF'
# You are on a voice call

You are Buddy, Claude on a live voice call with one person. Work exactly as you normally would as a coding agent: read, search, run commands, edit files when asked. The only difference is how you talk. Everything you want the person to hear goes inside `<say>` tags, and it is read aloud by a text to speech voice the moment you write it.

Every user message starts with a `[call · visual+audio]` or `[call · audio-only]` tag. If the person cut in on you, a `[cut in: …]` note says what they heard and what they missed.

## The tags

- `<say>…</say>` is spoken. Use as many as you need in one turn.
- `<screen>…</screen>` is shown on screen as markdown. It is for paths, code, diffs, tables and lists. Never use it in audio-only mode.
- Text outside tags is your working notes. It appears in a "behind the scenes" feed and is never spoken. Keep it brief.

## Talk while you work

The person is waiting on the line, and silence feels broken. Speak early and often, briefly.

- Before your first tool call, say in a few words what you are about to do: `<say>Let me look at the auth middleware.</say>`
- Between steps, give a one-line update when you learn something: `<say>Found the bug, it is in the token refresh. Checking the tests now.</say>`
- Do not narrate every tool call. One update every few steps is right.
- Then give the answer in a final `<say>`.

## How the answer sounds

- Lead with the verdict in the first sentence.
- Follow with two to four crisp points, one idea per sentence, 15 to 20 words at most.
- Sound like a sharp colleague on a call: plain words, warm, no filler, no preamble, no "Great question".
- No markdown, code, file paths, URLs or symbols inside `<say>`. Say file names as words, for example "auth dot ts".
- Say "cannot", not "can't". Round numbers: "about forty", not "41".
- Name at most three items, then summarise the rest: "and four smaller ones".
- End with a short hand-back: a question ("want me to fix it?") or a status ("done, over to you").
- In visual mode you may point at the screen ("the diff is on the right"). In audio-only mode never mention a screen; offer to save details to a file instead.

## Being cut in on

When the message has a `[cut in: …]` note:

- Do not repeat what they already heard.
- If they asked something new, answer that. Mention the unheard part only if it still matters, in one sentence.
- If they just said "pause" and then "go on", that is handled for you and you will not see it.
- If they say "shorter", give one or two sentences.

## When you change things

You may edit files and run commands as usual. Say what you are changing before you do it, in one sentence. Afterwards, say what changed in plain words and how you checked it. Never read code aloud.
EOF

import { ClaudeSession } from "./agent.ts";
import { clean } from "./cleaner.ts";
import { formatContext, type CallContext } from "./context.ts";
import { narrate, toolLabel } from "./narration.ts";
import { ReplyParser, type ParsedEvent } from "./parser.ts";
import { MoonshineSTT } from "./stt.ts";
import type { Mode, Rewriter } from "./types.ts";

const root = fileURLToPath(new URL("..", import.meta.url));
const webDir = join(root, "web");
const workDir = resolve(process.env.BUDDY_CWD ?? join(root, "session"));
const PORT = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const TYPES: Record<string, string> = { ".html": "text/html", ".js": "text/javascript", ".css": "text/css" };
const FILLER_MS = 2500;
const NARRATE_GAP_MS = 6000;

const systemPrompt = ["VOICE.md", "examples.md", "condensation.md"]
  .map((f) => readFileSync(join(root, "skill", "claude-call", f), "utf8"))
  .join("\n\n");

const rewriter: Rewriter = { toSpeech: async (x) => x };

let sttState: "loading" | "ready" | "error" = "loading";
const stt = new MoonshineSTT();
const sockets = new Set<WebSocket>();
stt.ready().then(
  () => { sttState = "ready"; console.log("Speech recognition ready"); },
  (e) => { sttState = "error"; console.error("Speech recognition failed to load:", e); },
).finally(() => { for (const ws of sockets) ws.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "stt", state: sttState })); });

const http = createServer(async (req, res) => {
  const path = normalize(req.url === "/" || !req.url ? "/index.html" : req.url.split("?")[0]).replace(/^(\.\.[/\\])+/, "");
  try {
    const body = await readFile(join(webDir, path));
    res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": TYPES[extname(path)] ?? "application/octet-stream", "cache-control": "no-cache" }).end(body);
  } catch {
    res.writeHead(404).end("not found");
  }
});

const wss = new WebSocketServer({ server: http });

wss.on("connection", (ws: WebSocket) => {
  sockets.add(ws);
  const send = (m: object) => ws.readyState === ws.OPEN && ws.send(JSON.stringify(m));
  send({ type: "stt", state: sttState });

  let mode: Mode = "visual";
  let agent: ClaudeSession | null = null;
  let segmentId: string | null = null;
  // per-turn speech state
  let parser = new ReplyParser();
  let lastSpokeAt = 0;
  let filler: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;

  const say = async (turn: number, text: string) => {
    const s = clean(await rewriter.toSpeech(text), mode);
    if (!s) return;
    lastSpokeAt = Date.now();
    clearTimeout(filler);
    send({ type: "say", turn, text: s });
  };

    for (const e of events) {
      if (e.kind === "sentence") await say(turn, e.text);
      else if (e.kind === "screen") send({ type: "screen", turn, text: e.text });
      else if (e.kind === "aside") send({ type: "aside", turn, text: e.text });

        for (const s of parts.slice(0, 2)) await say(turn, s.trim());
        if (parts.length > 2) send({ type: "screen", turn, text: e.text });
      }
    }
  };

    const a = new ClaudeSession({ cwd: workDir, systemPrompt, permissionMode: process.env.BUDDY_PERMISSION_MODE ?? "auto" });
    a.on((turn, ev) => {
      switch (ev.kind) {
        case "text": void handleParsed(turn, parser.feed(ev.text)); break;

Now the tests, updated for the new parser plus the context formatter.

Bash: cat > server/parser.test.ts <<'EOF' import { test } from "node:test"; import assert from "node:asser
cat > server/parser.test.ts <<'EOF'
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { ReplyParser, type ParsedEvent } from "./parser.ts";
import { clean } from "./cleaner.ts";
import { formatContext } from "./context.ts";

const run = (text: string, size = 3) => {
  const p = new ReplyParser();
  const ev: ParsedEvent[] = [];
  for (const ch of text.match(new RegExp(`[\\s\\S]{1,${size}}`, "g"))!) ev.push(...p.feed(ch));
  ev.push(...p.end());
  return ev;
};
const of = (ev: ParsedEvent[], kind: string) => ev.filter((e) => e.kind === kind).map((e) => e.text);

test("multiple say blocks stream sentences in order across chunk splits", () => {
  const ev = run("<say>Let me look.</say>\nReading auth.ts now\n<say>Found it. The fix is an await.\nWant more?</say>\n<screen>\nIn `a.ts`\n</screen>");
  assert.deepEqual(of(ev, "sentence"), ["Let me look.", "Found it.", "The fix is an await.", "Want more?"]);
  assert.equal(of(ev, "screen").join("").trim(), "In `a.ts`");
  assert.match(of(ev, "aside").join(""), /Reading auth\.ts now/);
  assert.equal(of(ev, "fallback").length, 0);
});

test("a say block without a closing period is still spoken when it closes", () => {
  assert.deepEqual(of(run("<say>Done, over to you</say>", 1), "sentence"), ["Done, over to you"]);
});

test("a stray < in working notes is not swallowed", () => {
  const ev = run("x < y and a<b\n<say>Ok.</say>", 2);
  assert.equal(of(ev, "aside").join(""), "x < y and a<b\n");
});

test("falls back when there is no say block", () => {
  const ev = run("Just plain text.");
  assert.deepEqual(of(ev, "fallback"), ["Just plain text."]);
});

test("cleaner", () => {
  assert.equal(clean("See `src/middleware/auth.ts` -> it can't use getUserById & more"), "See auth dot ts to it cannot use get User By Id and more");
  assert.equal(clean("Visit https://x.com now"), "Visit a link now");
  assert.match(clean("a\n```js\nx\n```\nb"), /code snippet on screen/);
});

test("call context", () => {
  assert.equal(formatContext("visual"), "[call · visual+audio]");
  const s = formatContext("audio", { kind: "paused", pausedMs: 6200, heard: "The cache is stale because", unheard: ["It never expires.", "Want the fix?"], working: true });
  assert.equal(s, '[call · audio-only] [cut in: the user said pause 6s ago; the last thing they heard was "The cache is stale because"; they did not hear 2 more sentences: "It never expires. Want the fix?"; your previous work was stopped]');
  assert.match(formatContext("visual", { kind: "interrupted" }), /talked over you/);
});

The server is ready. Now the browser side, starting with the voice module: a speech queue that can pause mid-sentence, resume at the same word, and report what you heard and what you missed.

Bash: cat > web/voice.js <<'EOF' // Buddy's mouth: a sentence queue on top of speechSynthesis that can sto
cat > web/voice.js <<'EOF'
// Buddy's mouth: a sentence queue on top of speechSynthesis that can stop mid-word,
// resume from the same word, and report exactly what the listener did and did not hear.

const words = (t) => t.toLowerCase().replace(/[^\w ]/g, " ").split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);

export class Voice {
  constructor({ onWord, onSentence, onIdle } = {}) {
    this.onWord = onWord ?? (() => {});
    this.onSentence = onSentence ?? (() => {});
    this.onIdle = onIdle ?? (() => {});
    this.queue = []; // { text, turn, record }
    this.current = null; // { text, turn, record, start, at, u }
    this.held = false;
    this.heard = []; // sentences fully heard in the current turn
    this.lastTurnSpoken = [];
    this.recent = new Set(); // words spoken lately, for the echo guard
    this.voice = null;
    const pick = () => {
      const vs = speechSynthesis.getVoices();
      this.voice = vs.find((v) => /Samantha/.test(v.name)) || vs.find((v) => /Google UK English Female/.test(v.name))
        || vs.find((v) => /Natural/.test(v.name) && v.lang.startsWith("en")) || vs.find((v) => v.lang.startsWith("en")) || null;
    };
    speechSynthesis.onvoiceschanged = pick;
    pick();
  }

  get busy() { return !!this.current || this.queue.length > 0; }
  get speaking() { return !!this.current; }

  /** Queue a sentence. record=false for fillers and narration that should not be replayed or reported. */
  say(text, turn, { record = true } = {}) {
    if (!record && (this.busy || this.held)) return; // fillers never pile up
    this.queue.push({ text, turn, record });
    words(text).forEach((w) => this.recent.add(w));
    this.#next();
  }

  /** Stop instantly but remember the position, so resume() picks up at the same word. */
  hold() {
    this.held = true;
    const c = this.current;
    if (!c) return;
    this.current = null;
    if (c.record) {
      const from = c.start + wordStart(c.text.slice(c.start), c.at);
      this.queue.unshift({ ...c, start: from });
    }
    this.queue = this.queue.filter((q) => q.record);
    speechSynthesis.cancel();
  }

  resume() {
    this.held = false;
    this.#next();
  }

  /** Drop everything: a new turn is starting. */
  clear() {
    this.held = false;
    this.queue = [];
    this.current = null;
    speechSynthesis.cancel();
  }

  newTurn() {
    if (this.heard.length) this.lastTurnSpoken = this.heard;
    this.heard = [];
    this.recent = new Set();
  }

  /** What the listener heard last and what they have not heard yet. */
  snapshot() {
    const pending = this.queue.filter((q) => q.record);
    const partial = pending[0] && pending[0].start > 0 ? pending[0].text.slice(0, pending[0].start).trim() : "";
    const heard = partial || this.heard[this.heard.length - 1] || "";
    const unheard = pending.map((q) => q.text.slice(q.start ?? 0).trim());
    return { heard, unheard };
  }

  isEcho(text) {
    const w = words(text);
    return w.length > 0 && w.filter((x) => this.recent.has(x)).length / w.length >= 0.7;
  }

  #next() {
    if (this.held || this.current) return;
    const item = this.queue.shift();
    if (!item) { this.onIdle(); return; }
    const start = item.start ?? 0;
    const c = { ...item, start, at: 0 };
    const u = new SpeechSynthesisUtterance(item.text.slice(start));
    if (this.voice) u.voice = this.voice;
    u.rate = 1.05;
    c.u = u;
    this.current = c;
    u.onboundary = (e) => {
      if (this.current !== c || e.name !== "word") return;
      c.at = e.charIndex;
      this.onWord(c.text, start + e.charIndex, e.charLength || 0);
    };
    const finish = () => {
      if (this.current !== c) return; // cancelled by hold() or clear()
      this.current = null;
      if (c.record) this.heard.push(c.text);
      this.#next();
    };
    u.onend = finish;
    u.onerror = finish;
    this.onSentence(c.text, start, c.record);
    speechSynthesis.speak(u);
  }
}

  onIdle: () => render(),
});

// ---------- view ----------
function render() {
  let s;
  if (!onCall) s = "asleep";

  else if (userPaused) s = "paused";

  else if (working) s = "thinking";

  document.body.classList.toggle("is-paused", userPaused);
  $("pauseBtn").textContent = userPaused ? "▶" : "⏸";

Now a proper streaming-safe markdown renderer in its own module, so I can unit-test it in Node.

Bash: cat > web/markdown.js <<'EOF' // Small markdown renderer for the behind-the-scenes panel. Safe to ca
cat > web/markdown.js <<'EOF'
// Small markdown renderer for the behind-the-scenes panel. Safe to call on a half-streamed
// document: an unclosed ``` fence renders as code so far, and whitespace inside code is kept
// exactly (indentation, blank lines, long lines scroll instead of wrapping).

export const esc = (s) => s.replace(/[&<>"]/g, (c) => ({ "&": "&amp;", "<": "&lt;", ">": "&gt;", '"': "&quot;" }[c]));

function inline(s) {
  // protect code spans first so their contents are not formatted
  const spans = [];
  let t = esc(s).replace(/`([^`\n]+)`/g, (_, c) => `\u0000${spans.push(c) - 1}\u0000`);
  t = t
    .replace(/\*\*([^*\n]+)\*\*/g, "<b>$1</b>")
    .replace(/(^|[\s(])\*([^*\n]+)\*(?=[\s).,;:!?]|$)/g, "$1<i>$2</i>")
    .replace(/\[([^\]\n]+)\]\((?:[^)\s]+)\)/g, "<u>$1</u>");
  return t.replace(/\u0000(\d+)\u0000/g, (_, i) => `<code>${spans[i]}</code>`);
}

const isTableRow = (l) => /^\s*\|.*\|\s*$/.test(l);
const isRule = (l) => /^\s*\|?\s*:?-{2,}:?\s*(\|\s*:?-{2,}:?\s*)*\|?\s*$/.test(l);
const cells = (l) => l.trim().replace(/^\||\|$/g, "").split("|").map((c) => inline(c.trim()));

export function renderMarkdown(src) {
  const lines = src.replace(/\r\n?/g, "\n").split("\n");
  const out = [];
  let i = 0;
  while (i < lines.length) {
    const line = lines[i];
    const fence = /^\s*(```|~~~)\s*([\w+-]*)\s*$/.exec(line);
    if (fence) {
      const body = [];
      i++;
      while (i < lines.length && !new RegExp(`^\\s*${fence[1]}\\s*$`).test(lines[i])) body.push(lines[i++]);
      i++; // closing fence (or end of a still-streaming block)
      const lang = fence[2] ? ` data-lang="${esc(fence[2])}"` : "";
      out.push(`<pre${lang}><code>${esc(body.join("\n"))}</code></pre>`);
      continue;
    }
    if (isTableRow(line) && i + 1 < lines.length && isRule(lines[i + 1])) {
      const head = cells(line);
      i += 2;
      const rows = [];
      while (i < lines.length && isTableRow(lines[i])) rows.push(cells(lines[i++]));
      out.push(`<div class="tbl"><table><thead><tr>${head.map((c) => `<th>${c}</th>`).join("")}</tr></thead><tbody>${rows.map((r) => `<tr>${r.map((c) => `<td>${c}</td>`).join("")}</tr>`).join("")}</tbody></table></div>`);
      continue;
    }
    const h = /^(#{1,6})\s+(.*)$/.exec(line);
    if (h) { out.push(`<div class="h h${h[1].length}">${inline(h[2])}</div>`); i++; continue; }
    const li = /^(\s*)([-*+]|\d+[.)])\s+(.*)$/.exec(line);
    if (li) {
      const ordered = /\d/.test(li[2]);
      const items = [];
      while (i < lines.length) {
        const m = /^(\s*)([-*+]|\d+[.)])\s+(.*)$/.exec(lines[i]);
        if (!m) break;
        const depth = Math.min(4, Math.floor(m[1].replace(/\t/g, "  ").length / 2));
        items.push(`<li style="margin-left:${depth * 1.2}em"${/\d/.test(m[2]) ? ` value="${parseInt(m[2])}"` : ""}>${inline(m[3])}</li>`);
        i++;
      }
      out.push(ordered ? `<ol>${items.join("")}</ol>` : `<ul>${items.join("")}</ul>`);
      continue;
    }
    if (!line.trim()) { i++; continue; }
    const para = [];
    while (i < lines.length && lines[i].trim() && !/^\s*(```|~~~)/.test(lines[i]) && !/^#{1,6}\s/.test(lines[i]) && !/^(\s*)([-*+]|\d+[.)])\s+/.test(lines[i]) && !isTableRow(lines[i])) para.push(inline(lines[i++]));
    out.push(`<p>${para.join("<br>")}</p>`);
  }
  return out.join("");
}
EOF
cat > web/markdown.test.js <<'EOF'
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { renderMarkdown } from "./markdown.js";

test("code fences keep indentation, blank lines and long lines verbatim", () => {
  const code = "def f(x):\n    if x:\n\n        return '<a & b>'" + " ".repeat(3) + "x".repeat(200);
  const html = renderMarkdown("Here:\n```python\n" + code + "\n```\nafter");
  assert.match(html, /<pre data-lang="python"><code>def f\(x\):\n    if x:\n\n        return '&lt;a &amp; b&gt;' {3}x{200}<\/code><\/pre>/);
  assert.match(html, /<p>after<\/p>$/);
  assert.doesNotMatch(html, /<br>.*<\/code>/s);
});

56:Voice input works like a call: no wake word, no key. Once started, the mic stays open and everything the user says is sent to Claude.
57:
58:- **Manual start.** The user starts a window with a button. Outside a window the recognizer is off, so there is no background battery drain.
59:- **Continuous listening.** Short pauses are merged into one turn (about 1.2 seconds of silence ends it). The mic restarts itself whenever the browser ends recognition.
60:- **Sleep timer.** The window ends after `sleepMinutes` (default 15, user-adjustable, 2 to 60) with no speech from the user. If Buddy is mid-reply, the timer waits until the reply ends plus 30 seconds.
61:- **Loud sleep.** On expiry Buddy says "going to sleep, press start to wake me" and the indicator goes gray. Saying "go to sleep" ends the window immediately.
62:- **Echo guard.** The mic also hears the speakers, so transcripts that mostly repeat what Buddy just said are ignored. Headphones are recommended.

- `Agent` cannot be swapped to another model: Claude Code runs Claude. What you can swap is the underlying auth (subscription login vs an API key) by setting or unsetting `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the se
- Keeping the interfaces in from Day 1 costs almost nothing and is painful to retrofit later.

## Three-day plan

## Risks and mitigations

## Demo script

## Post-prototype roadmap
Buddy is a local app that lets you talk to Claude Code and hear it talk back. You hold a key, say what you want, and Buddy forwards it to a Claude Code session running on your subscription. Replies come back as speech, with an on-screen text panel in visual mode and no panel in audio-only mode. A `claude-call` skill reshapes each reply into something that works for the ear instead of the eye.
The prototype has three days to prove the loop end to end: say "Buddy" in a listening window, Claude Code answers, Buddy speaks a short sensible reply, the user can interrupt, and the whole thing runs on the existing Claude subscription with no extra API keys. It is scoped to discussion and planning, not file edits, so it needs no approval UI in v0. Success is a two-minute live demo where a non-technical observer can follow the conversation.
The top row carries your voice to Claude; the middle row carries Claude's reply back out as speech. The server is a thin Node process that owns the WebSocket to the page and spawns one `claude -p` child per conversation, resuming it with `--resume` between turns. Everything in the top and middle rows is yours; `claude -p` is unchanged, with the `claude-call` skill picked up from the server's working directory. The screen panel is only shown in Visual+Audio mode and reads the `<screen>` block from each reply.

Now rewriting the spec sections to match what was built, keeping them short. The empty plan, risks, demo and roadmap sections stay as they are.

body=r'''## Overview

Buddy is a local app that puts you on a voice call with Claude Code. You start a call, talk normally, and Buddy talks back while Claude works: a short line before it digs in, quick updates between steps, then a crisp spoken answer. A "behind the scenes" panel shows Claude's thinking, tool calls and detail as they happen. Everything runs on the existing Claude subscription, with no API keys.

The prototype proves the call loop end to end: natural turn-taking with no cut-offs, speech that starts while Claude is still working, "pause" and "go on", and cutting in with a new question, where Claude is told what you heard and what you missed. Success is a two-minute live demo where a non-technical observer can follow the conversation.

## Scope

In scope for v0:

- A call started from a local web page (Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox). The mic stays open for the call, with no wake word and no key.
- Voice activity detection in the browser (Silero VAD) to find where you start and stop. Speech-to-text on the server (Moonshine, running on CPU), with no key and no cloud.
- One warm `claude -p` process per call, fed by stream-json, in `auto` permission mode, so Claude works as a normal agent.
- Speech through the browser's `speechSynthesis`, sentence by sentence as Claude writes.
- Pause, resume, cut-in with context, the local commands, and the sleep timer.
- A live behind-the-scenes panel, hidden in audio-only mode.

Out of scope for v0:

- A VS Code extension
- Neural or cloud voices (the `TTS` interface allows them later)
- Voice-driven approvals: `auto` mode decides, and anything it blocks is reported, not asked
- Memory across calls, packaging, auth, multi-user

## Architecture

&#91;embedded content: Buddy pipeline · 9 components, one Claude Code session\]

- **Page:** the VAD cuts your speech into utterances and sends each one as 16 kHz audio over the WebSocket. The page owns the call state (listening, hearing, working, speaking, paused) and the speech queue.
- **Server:** a thin Node process. It transcribes each utterance with Moonshine (about 0.2 to 0.5 s) and keeps one warm `claude -p --input-format stream-json` per call. The server streams Claude's output back as typed events: `say`, `screen`, `aside`, `thinking`, `tool` and `tool_result`.
- **Warm process:** it removes the cold start from every turn after the first. Interrupts use the stream-json `interrupt` control request, so the session and its context survive.
- **Working directory:** `BUDDY_CWD`, default `session/`.

## Interaction model

One person, one mic, one conversation. The orb and its label always show the state: `asleep`, `listening`, `hearing you`, `working`, `speaking`, `paused`.

The call:

- **Start and sleep.** Press call to start. The call sleeps after `sleepMinutes` with no speech from you (default 15, adjustable 2 to 60). Buddy says so out loud; "go to sleep" or the end button ends it at once. The mic is off outside a call.
- **Turn-taking.** The VAD ends your utterance after about 0.9 s of silence and sends it at once. If you keep talking within 1.5 s, before Buddy has spoken, that turn is replaced by one with your whole sentence. A pause mid-thought never cuts you off, and quick questions still get quick answers.
- **Talking while working.** Claude speaks a short `<say>` line before its first tool call and between steps. If nothing has been said after 3.5 s, Buddy says "one sec"; long silent stretches get a short narration such as "reading auth dot ts".
- **Pause.** "Pause", "wait", "hold on" or the space bar stops the voice mid-word. Claude keeps working, and its output queues up. "Go on" resumes from the same word.
- **Cut in.** Anything else said over Buddy stops the voice and the running turn. Your words go to Claude with a note: what you last heard, what you did not hear, how long ago you paused, and whether work wa

Buddy now works like a call. It runs on port 3200 with all the changes, and the 11 unit tests pass. In headless Chromium with a fake mic playing a speech clip, the whole loop worked. A real mic and Safari are still untested.

What it does - Turn-taking: you just talk. Buddy waits for about 0.9 s of silence before treating you as done. If you keep going within 1.5 s, before Buddy has spoken, your two parts are joined into one message to Claude. The test clip's mid-sentence pause no longer split the turn. - Speed: each call keeps one Claude process running, so after the first turn there is no startup wait. In tests, Buddy's first spoken line came about 2.5 s after the question, and a cut-in got its answer about 1.6 s later. - Talking while working: Claude says a short line before it starts ("Reading sample dot py now"), gives updates between steps, then a crisp answer. Long silences get "one sec" or a short narration. - Pause: "pause", "wait", "hold on" or the space bar stops Buddy mid-word while Claude keeps working. "Go on" resumes from the same word. If you say something else instead, Claude gets a note with what you last heard, what you missed, how long ago you paused, and whether its work was stopped. - Behind the scenes: a live panel shows Claude's thinking, its notes, and tool cards that expand to the exact command and output. Code keeps its exact indentation, long lines scroll inside their own box, and the page had zero horizontal overflow in the test. - Permissions: Claude runs in auto mode, as you asked.

Changed from the plan - Transcription runs on this server, not in your browser. It's the same Moonshine model, about 0.2–0.5 s per utterance, with no key and no cloud. Your laptop only loads the small model that detects when you stop talking (~2 MB), served from this server. - Turn merging is new: I added the 1.5 s merge after the test showed pauses splitting turns.

Browsers: Buddy no longer uses Chrome's speech recognition, so Safari, Firefox and Edge should work too. Safari needs audio and speech to start inside the click on Call, and that is handled. Firefox on Linux often has no speech voices installed. Only headless Chromium has actually been tested.

Untested risks - Speakers: Buddy's voice can reach your mic. On speakers it waits for the transcript before reacting and ignores its own echoed words, which works but is slower to interrupt. Turn on the headphones toggle to get instant interruption. - Where Claude works: Claude edits files in session/ by default. To point it at a real project, start the server with BUDDY_CWD=/path/to/project PORT=3200 npm start.

Spec: I rewrote SPEC.md to match what was built, removed the duplicate headings, and shortened it from about 210 lines to 130. The three-day plan, risks, demo and roadmap sections are still empty.

To try it, reload http://localhost:3200 through your tunnel and press the call button. Talk naturally, then try "pause" and "go on" while it answers.

Yes, the gap between the text and the voice really did get bigger, and it was my doing. I've fixed that and made the context changes you asked for. All 187 tests pass, but I haven't heard any of this on a live call yet. Voice lagging behind the text "Stereo voices" was on by default. With it on, the server makes every sentence as audio using macOS say, which takes 2–2.5 seconds per sentence on this machine. The text showed up straight away while the voice trailed behind. Before that, the browser spoke instantly. Now, if a sentence's audio isn't ready within 0.35 s, the browser says it instead. It's the same Mac voice, just from the centre rather than the agent's side. The server also starts making the next few sentences while the current one plays, so later ones are more likely to come out panned. If you'd rather have no gap and no panning at all, turn off Stereo voices in Settings. Context: different for Ada and for the agents Before, two-thirds of every message Ada got was the same full team list, repeated each turn. Her conversation also started from scratch on every server restart, so she forgot everything, including what mattered. Ada: - Only changes: she gets the full team once at the start. After that she only gets [team changes since your last message: …], or nothing if nothing changed. She gets the full list again every 15 turns, and right after Claude Code summarises (compacts) her conversation. - Fresh conversation on each server start: her day-to-day chatter ("go to Juno", "pause") isn't carried forward. What matters is kept in a notebook, ~/buddy-home/.buddy/ada-notebook.json, which she is shown at the start of each conversation. It holds: - things you asked her to remember (she now has <remember> and <forget> tags), such as "we went with Postgres" - each project's latest report, one line per project - recent events, logged automatically: project set up or opened, work handed out, project closed Project agents: - They keep their full sessions, because their history is the actual work. - The call header is now sent only when it changes, not on every turn. - Their prompt now says that if their conversation is summarised, they should keep decisions, files changed and open questions, and drop the call chatter. The main changes are in the new server/notebook.ts and in server/call.ts, with tests in server/notebook.test.ts. To try it: the server running on port 3000 (pid 51029, the one you started) is still on the old code. Restart it to pick up these changes, then reload the page. Nothing is committed yet.

Running the full test suite one last time, then stopping my test server and committing:
Ran 2 shell commands
ClaudeCall can now be installed as an app on a phone, iPad or laptop, and run in the background on macOS or Linux. Everything is committed locally in two commits, nothing pushed, both authored by Palak: - 552c96a: all the earlier work, including the voice-gap fix and Ada's notebook - a1f85c1: the deployment work Your more_features.txt notes are left out. All 188 tests pass. App on phone, iPad and laptop - It can be added to the home screen or dock and opens full screen with its own icon. If the computer is asleep or unreachable, it shows a "can't reach your computer" page instead of a browser error. - Layout: I took screenshots at 8 sizes, from phone to laptop. Nothing scrolls sideways and the page shows no errors. - Phone, iPad held upright and small windows: one section at a time, with tabs at the bottom. - Phone on its side: the call card goes side by side, so the controls fit without scrolling. - Small laptop and iPad landscape: two columns, the call on the left and the canvas on the right. - The "Choose folder" button now only appears on the computer running ClaudeCall. On a phone it would have opened Finder on your laptop. macOS and Linux - Background service: npm run service install sets it up (add -- --lan for phones on your Wi-Fi). It starts at login, restarts if it stops, and keeps the same access code. It also has status, logs, restart and uninstall. - Linux: I checked it in a clean Linux container. It installed, the tests passed, the server started, speech recognition loaded and the page and connection worked. Stereo voices and "Test how it's heard" use macOS's own voices, so they're hidden on Linux. Phones: the README explains two ways to get the secure address the microphone needs: - Tailscale (recommended): a real certificate, and it works away from home. You run tailscale serve --bg 3000 on the computer. - Same Wi-Fi: a certificate ClaudeCall makes itself, accepted once on each device. Not tested yet: - I didn't run the service install on your Mac, because it would clash with the server you're running on port 3000. Linux was only tested in a container, without systemd or a real claude. - I haven't tried it on a real iPhone or iPad. To try it, stop your current server (it's still on the old code) and run npm run service install -- --lan. It prints the address and code to open on your phone. I can do that step for you if you want.

Yes, there's a DMG now: dist/ClaudeCall-0.1.0-arm64.dmg (221 MB), built and tested. All three requests are done and committed locally as 48ec132; 188 tests pass and nothing is pushed. DMG. You drag ClaudeCall to Applications and open it. That does three things: - starts ClaudeCall in the background and keeps it running after login - opens it in your browser, already past the access-code screen - uses its own copy of Node, so the Mac doesn't need Node installed I tested the real app from the DMG on a separate port with a throwaway home folder, and it all worked: the server started, the speech model downloaded to the app's cache folder, and the page opened straight into the call. Testing found and fixed two bugs, one with folder paths containing spaces and one with a disk image left attached after a failed build. The test setup is removed. You can rebuild it with npm run build:mac. Limits: - Apple silicon only. An Intel version has to be built on an Intel Mac. - No Apple Developer ID. The first time, right-click → Open. Signing it properly needs a paid Apple developer account. Claude Code. The requirement is now on the opening page and in the README. After connecting, ClaudeCall checks whether Claude Code is installed and signed in, and if not shows a setup screen: - Not installed: the install command with a copy button, plus the npm alternative. - Not signed in: "Sign in with Claude" or "Use Anthropic Console" opens Claude Code's own sign-in in a terminal, so ClaudeCall never sees your password. It notices when you're done and closes the screen. - From a phone: it shows the command to run on the computer instead. - API key: you can paste one instead of signing in. It's saved readable only by you. I tested the "not installed" screen and the normal signed-in case. I didn't click the sign-in buttons for real, because that would change how your own Claude Code is signed in, and I didn't try a real API key. Opening page: - an animated diagram: Ada in the middle, team members connecting with pulses running along the links, gentle voice ripples - the headline "Lead your Claude team by voice" and a short pitch - example commands typed out one after another - three feature cards and the access-code card On phones the code box comes right after the pitch. Animation is turned off for people who've switched off motion in their system settings. Two other things: - Your old server isn't running. The one on port 3000 had already exited; I didn't stop it. Opening the new app (or running npm run service install) starts the new version. - Linux has no package yet. It runs from source or as a service, but there's no AppImage or .deb like the DMG. I can build one next if you want.

how can i do it via github actions, so that the dmg, linux image, app for pther phone ipad etc, are built there itself
Claude's response
GitHub Actions can build the Mac and Linux versions. Phones and iPads are different: the installable app there is the web app your computer serves, so there's nothing to build for them. Native App Store or Play Store apps would need developer accounts and signing keys, which is your decision; more on that at the end. To keep CI simple, I'll make each build script able to target either processor from one machine (Apple silicon and Intel for Mac, x64 and arm64 for Linux).     76  
    77 +**Android release key (optional).** Without one, each APK is si
       +gned with a throwaway key: it                                  
    78 +installs, but a newer version won't install over an older one. 
       +To fix that, make a key once and                               
    79 +keep it safe. Losing it means users have to uninstall before up
       +dating.                                                        
    80 +                                                               
    81 +```sh                                                          
    82 +keytool -genkeypair -v -keystore claudecall.jks -alias claudeca
       +ll -keyalg RSA -keysize 4096 -validity 10000                   
    83 +base64 -i claudecall.jks | pbcopy      # on Linux: base64 -w0 c
       +laudecall.jks                                                  
    84 +```                                                            
    85 +

       -m." Never ask "are you sure?" yourself, before or after: that w

       -e lead chose to keep…]` note tells you how it went.

    22  - `<delegate to="rex">task</delegate>` — hand an agent work in 
        the background. If it is busy, the task waits behind its curren
        t work; nothing is interrupted.
    23  - `<switch to="rex"/>` — give an agent the floor.
    24  - `<park to="rex"/>` — stop an agent, keeping its conversation.
         `<close to="rex"/>` takes it off the team; its folder stays. C
        losing cannot be undone, so ClaudeCall itself asks the lead to 
        confirm it. When they ask you to close an agent, write the tag 
        straight away and say nothing about confirming: ClaudeCall puts
         the question to them in your voice right after. Never ask "are
         you sure?" yourself, before or after: that would make them con
        firm twice. A `[the lead confirmed…]` or `[the lead chose to ke
        ep…]` note tells you how it went.
    25 +- Always finish a tag with its closing tag (`</new>`, `</open>`
       +, `</delegate>`), even after a long brief.                     
    26  - Every tag is carried out as soon as you write it, even if the
         lead cuts in while you are still talking. Switching the floor 
        and call controls wait until your turn ends.
    27  
    28  Add `focus="true"` to `new`, `open` or `delegate` to give that 
        agent the floor as it starts.

The "New Agents forming" commit is done (cb95c4a). It's an empty checkpoint commit, because everything was already committed in c668c76. This fix is aef9794 on top of it. Why you couldn't interrupt. When I fixed the dropped actions earlier, I made talking over a busy Ada go to her as a side question (Claude Code's /btw) instead of stopping her. Nothing got lost, but she never actually stopped, so it felt like she ignored you. How it works now: - Talking over Ada cuts her off for real, and nothing is dropped. Anything she had already set up still happens (starting an agent, handing out work). If you cut in while she was in the middle of writing one, the same message that interrupts her tells her it didn't happen, so she redoes it. - A "switch you to Juno" she'd queued is skipped once you cut in, since you were just talking to her, and she's told. - Project agents busy with real work still get your words as a side question, so talking never kills their work, as you asked before. - Her voice gives way straight away. On speakers, it drops to a whisper the moment you start talking, then stops once your words are in, or comes back up if it was only noise or her own echo. With the Bluetooth switch on (headphones), she stops instantly. Tested live: five seconds into a slow weather lookup, I cut in with "make an agent called Bo". Ada stopped the lookup, and Bo was on the team 2.4 seconds later. Not tested: I can't try the voice dip with a real microphone myself. It only works with the Mac voices, which are on by default ("Voices placed left and right" in Settings). With the browser's built-in voice instead, she keeps talking at full volume until your words are in.

What the .deb does: - installs to /opt/claudecall, with a claudecall command and an app-menu entry - on first open, sets up the user's background service, the same way the Mac app does - installing a newer .deb moves anyone already running ClaudeCall onto the new version Tested on Ubuntu 24.04 and Debian 12: install, first launch as a normal user, upgrade while running, and removal. The x64 one was tested on GitHub's machine; I couldn't run it on this Mac. Bugs found along the way, all fixed: - The first Mac-built .deb wouldn't install at all, because macOS's archive format breaks Debian's installer. - apt refused to upgrade between two builds of the same version. Each build now gets a higher version number. - The first-launch set-up failed on a missing $USER. - Four CI failures, all mine: a shutdown exit code in the start-up check, an option the Linux tar lacks, a timing race on the slow emulated machine, and the same Mac tar options again. New docs: - README.md is now the install guide for someone downloading the DMG or .deb. It covers installing, setting up Claude Code, using ClaudeCall, phones, updating, uninstalling and troubleshooting. - The build and release details are in DEVELOPMENT.md. One step left: the README points people to the GitHub Releases page, and that's still empty. Publishing a release means pushing a version tag, for example git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0. The workflow then attaches the DMG, both .deb files, the .tar.xz files and the APK. That makes them public, so I haven't done it. Shall I?
